table.brief: Three-level column header (Region > Country > Q1/Q2) with a corner cell spanning 3 header rows

understanding.purpose: Compare quarterly solar PV capacity additions (MW) for 2024 across five market segments and four countries, including Q1→Q2 movement and quarterly totals. It is a reference/comparison table, read row-wise (one segment across all countries) and pair-wise (Q1 vs Q2 within a country).
understanding.reading: A reader anchors on the row label (segment), then sweeps right to compare the same segment across Germany, France, Japan and Australia, and compares the adjacent Q1/Q2 pair to see quarterly growth. Totals are read last as a column summary. Alignment is numeric/right, so columns must be at least wide enough that four-digit values with thousands separators never wrap or truncate; country and quarter headers are short and must stay on one line.
groups: Col 1: row-label column (Segment) — a single anchor column, must be readable as a unit
Cols 2–3: Germany Q1/Q2 — an inseparable comparison pair
Cols 2–5 together form the Europe block; cols 6–9 form the Asia-Pacific block, so the boundary between col 5 and col 6 should read as the strongest internal break
keep_intact: All MW values, especially 4-digit totals (2,065 / 2,330 / 1,232 / 1,803) — never wrap or clip
Country names Germany / France / Japan / Australia
The row-label words 'Commercial', 'industrial', 'Residential', 'Utility-scale', 'Community' must not break mid-word
may_wrap: Row-label phrases in col 1 ('Residential rooftop', 'Commercial & industrial', 'Utility-scale', 'Community solar') can break at the space/ampersand into two lines, absorbing extra height in already-tall body rows
Nothing in cols 2–9 should wrap; those columns are numeric and must stay one line

preferred.name: r1B
preferred.note: Explore the opposite extreme: all eight numeric columns identical at 62px, so every value sits on the same rhythm with a 3px safety margin over the 40px worst case, and the grid is unambiguously regular. Col 1 shrinks to 109px (content 88px, still above the 86px longest label word, so no mid-word split) but every label except 'Utility-scale' wraps, producing a nearly uniform 60px body rhythm. This tests whether an even row rhythm beats a roomy label column.

preferred.name: r3C
preferred.note: Push every numeric column to 62px and take the 8px from col1. All numeric cells then have 41px of text, the most breathing room for 4-digit totals; each country group spans 124px and both regions 248px. Col1 at 109px still has 88px of text, 2px above the 86px 'Utility-scale' minimum, and remains below the 'Commercial &' orphan threshold.

acceptable.name: r2C
acceptable.note: New idea: use width itself to make the Europe / Asia-Pacific break visible in the body, not just in the header. The Europe block is 4 × 62 = 248px and the Asia-Pacific block 4 × 60 = 240px, so there is a step at the col 5 / col 6 boundary that no other pair boundary has, while Q1/Q2 inside each country remain exactly equal. The 2px trimmed from each Asia-Pacific column (Japan and Australia peak at 38px, not 40px) funds a label column of 117px (96px content), so labels breathe and every numeric column keeps at least 1px of slack.

acceptable.name: r3A
acceptable.note: Keep r2C's safe col1 at 117px (96px text, safely below the 'Commercial &' orphan threshold) and equalize all eight numeric columns at 61px. This removes the Europe/Asia 8px imbalance: each country group spans 122px and each region 244px. At 61px every numeric cell has 40px of text, enough for 4-digit totals, while col1 stays comfortably above the 86px 'Utility-scale' minimum.

acceptable.name: r3B
acceptable.note: Keep r2A's known-good 118px label column and equalize the numeric columns at 61px, taking the single 1px reduction from Australia Q1, which holds only the 3-digit 965. This gives the wrapped row labels slightly more air without risking any 4-digit value; Europe spans 244px and Asia-Pacific 243px, effectively balanced.

acceptable.name: r2A
acceptable.note: Content-driven sizing instead of a flat grid: Germany gets 62/62 (41px content vs its 40px totals), France and Japan 61/61 (40px vs 38px), Australia 59/60 because its widest value is only 38px (Q1 needs just 28px). That recovers 9px for the label column, taking it from 88px to 97px of content — enough that 'Residential', 'Commercial' and 'Community' sit comfortably rather than being pinched. Every numeric column now has at least 1px of slack, so no total can clip. Pairs stay equal within each country, so Q1/Q2 comparison is unaffected.

acceptable.name: r2B
acceptable.note: Pushes the label column to 123px (102px of content) because row labels are the anchor a reader lands on first and are the only cells that wrap; France, Japan and Australia give up 2–3px each since their widest values (33–38px) still fit with 1–2px to spare, while Germany keeps 62/62 to protect the 40px totals 2,065/2,330. The result is a calmer left column and a numeric block that no longer looks starved.

bad.name: r1A
bad.note: Keep r0B's space-efficient minimums but enforce equality within each Q1/Q2 pair and across country blocks: Germany 61/61 (its 2,065/2,330 need 40px content) and all other data columns 59 (exactly the 38px needed by 1,232/1,055). The label column gets the remaining 129px — the most it can have while every pair stays equal, so 'Utility-scale' still fits on one line. This removes r0B's ragged pairs and r0C's mid-number splits in one move.
bad.why: The eight quarter columns drop to 59px, leaving only 38px of text width for four-digit totals such as "2,065" and "1,055" (≈40px needed); in the rendered Total row the figures press against the cell borders, and the 129px Segment column wastes space that the numeric columns actually need.

bad.name: contrast
bad.note: Plausible-looking because the numeric columns are generous and uniform, but the Segment column gives only 64px of text width — less than the 86px word "Residential" — so row labels break mid-word ("Residenti/al") and the first column stops reading as a clean stack of category names.
bad.why: Plausible-looking because the numeric columns are generous and uniform, but the Segment column gives only 64px of text width — less than the 86px word "Residential" — so row labels break mid-word ("Residenti/al") and the first column stops reading as a clean stack of category names.

rationale: This table is read two ways: down the Segment column to find a technology, then across paired Q1/Q2 cells to compare quarters, so the eight quarter columns are peers and should be uniform while the label column only needs to hold its longest word intact. A 109px Segment column keeps "Residential" and "Commercial" whole on the first line and lets the second word drop cleanly, while 62px per quarter column gives 41px of text — just enough for the widest four-digit total with a hair of clearance. r1B and r3C are numerically the same design and both read calmly; r1A's 59px quarter columns visibly squeeze the totals row. The merged two-level header (continent › country › quarter) already carries the grouping, so no extra width is needed to signal it — even column rhythm does that job better than a wide first column.

general: Columns that play the same role (here Q1 vs Q2 across countries) should be equal width; the reader compares them pairwise and any wobble reads as noise.
Size the numeric columns to the widest value in the body — including the total row — not to the header; headers can wrap, numbers cannot.
A row-header column needs only enough width for its longest unbreakable word plus a little air; giving it more steals from the data columns without improving legibility.
specific: Because continent and country grouping is already expressed by merged header cells, the Segment column does not need to be visually dominant here.
Four-digit values with thousands separators (2,065; 1,055) are the binding constraint on this table's quarter-column width, at roughly 40px of content.
Row heights of 60px occur only for the two wrapped segment labels; keeping those wraps at word boundaries (not mid-word) is what makes the two-line rows acceptable.

tradeoffs: One could argue for a wider Segment column (121–129px) so labels like "Commercial & industrial" sit closer to one line and the table has a stronger left anchor, accepting slightly narrower quarter columns; equally, a 61px quarter column is defensible if you prefer maximum label comfort over numeric clearance.
uncertain: Whether 59–61px quarter columns actually clip or merely look tight depends on the rendering engine's rounding of comma-digit widths; a designer with different font metrics might accept r1A, and the difference between 61 and 62px is below the threshold of conscious perception.

critique.good: The numeric grid is perfectly regular: all eight data columns are 61px, so every Q1/Q2 pair and every country block is exactly the same width. Values sit on a consistent rhythm, nothing wraps, no header wraps, no mid-word splits, and the Europe/Asia-Pacific boundary at col5/col6 reads cleanly. Row-wise scanning across countries is easy because each logical column occupies the same visual slot.
critique.problems: The label column is visibly cramped next to generously wide number columns — poor proportion between the anchor column and the data columns. Three labels wrap to two lines, so row heights are mixed (36/60) and the table is the tallest of the three (361px), with a slightly ragged left edge of stacked two-line labels.
critique.cause: Col 1 = 117px (content 96px) is below the ~172px one-line width, so 'Residential rooftop', 'Commercial & industrial' and 'Community solar' break to two lines, while the 61px number columns hold values like 55 and 965 with a lot of leftover air.

critique.good: Shortest table (338px) and the most comfortable label column: at 144px only two labels wrap, so the left edge reads as a clean list of segment names. All numbers stay on one line and both group headers still sit correctly over their blocks.
critique.problems: The numeric columns are ragged: France is 54/59, Australia 49/59, Germany 61/61. The Q1/Q2 pairs no longer read as units, the same logical column lands at different x-positions across countries, and the Australia block is visibly narrower than Japan's, which unbalances the Asia-Pacific block. Narrow columns beside tight ones create uneven internal white space.
critique.cause: Widths were set to each column's individual minimum (54px for France Q1's 33px content, 49px for Australia Q1's 28px content) instead of per pair/role, and the 13px saved was spent on col 1 = 144px.

critique.good: Germany's 65px columns give the four-digit numbers noticeable air, the label column at 129px keeps 'Segment' and the country headers clear, and the three-level header stack reads well.
critique.problems: Two totals are split mid-number ('1,23 / 2' in France Q2 and '1,05 / 5' in Australia Q2) — a data-integrity failure that makes the table look broken and invites misreading. Row heights are uneven across all four body rows, and the two 65px columns waste 4px each.
critique.cause: Col 5 = 58px (content 37px) and col 9 = 52px (content 31px) fall below the 38px one-line requirement for '1,232' and '1,055', while cols 2–3 were over-allocated at 65px when 61px was sufficient.

critique.good: The row-label column is genuinely comfortable: 129px gives 108px of content, so 'Residential rooftop' and 'Commercial & industrial' break at the space and read as clean two-line units. Equal Q1/Q2 widths inside every country keep the pairs symmetric, so a reader can compare quarters without the geometry fighting them, and the merged three-tier header (Segment / Europe / Germany / Q1) stays perfectly legible with no wrapping (0/15).
critique.problems: Every numeric column is running at or below the width of its widest value. Germany (61px = 40px content) holds totals 2,065 and 2,330, which are exactly 40px; France Q2 (59px = 38px content) holds 1,232, exactly 38px. That is zero slack on the four-digit totals — the single most important row in the table. Any rounding, font substitution or kerning difference clips or wraps a total, which is the worst possible failure here. The layout is also lopsided: a 129px label column against 59–61px numerics is a 2.2:1 ratio, and 108px of content is spent on words that only need 86px, while the columns that carry the actual data are starved.
critique.cause: The label column took 129 of the 605px, leaving 476px for eight numeric columns (59.5px average). Because the widest numeric content is 40px and padding is 21px, 61px is the absolute floor and 59px is already below what France Q2 and Australia Q2 need.

critique.good: This is the safer of the two: 62px everywhere gives 41px of content, so 2,065 / 2,330 / 1,803 all have a pixel of clearance and the totals row is protected. The eight numeric columns are perfectly even, so the rhythm of Q1/Q2 pairs is regular and the numbers read as a clean matrix; nothing wraps and there are no mid-word splits.
critique.problems: The cost is paid entirely by the label column. At 109px it shows 88px of content, only 2px above the longest unbreakable word (86px — 'Residential', 'Commercial', 'Utility-scale'). Every body label is forced onto two lines, three rows become 60px tall, and the left column visibly strains against its border. Worse, the even 62px grid erases the one internal break the table is supposed to signal: the Europe / Asia-Pacific boundary between col 5 and col 6 looks identical to the France/Japan pair boundary, so the block structure survives only in the header, not in the body.
critique.cause: The 605px budget caps the numeric columns at 62px each (8 × 62 = 496), which pins the label at 109px — the mathematical minimum is 107px, so there is no room left to give the labels air or to vary widths for grouping.

critique.good: Best label-column behaviour: col1 at 118px gives 97px of text, enough for 'Commercial' but not 'Commercial &', so the ampersand is not stranded. 'Utility-scale' stays intact, all headers are one line, and 4-digit totals fit.
critique.problems: The eight numeric columns jitter between 59 and 62px, so they do not read as an even rhythm. Col8 is narrowest at 59px yet holds only 965, while col4 at 61px carries 1,115. Europe spans 247px versus Asia-Pacific 241px.
critique.cause: Leftover pixels were distributed ad hoc. Col1 at 118px happens to sit below the 'Commercial &' line-break threshold; the 59–62px spread across cols 2–9 creates the uneven regional blocks.

critique.good: Col1 at 123px gives row labels more air; numeric columns are mostly 60–62px; no headers wrap and no mid-word splits occur.
critique.problems: The extra 5px in col1 lets 'Commercial &' sit on the first line, leaving the ampersand dangling at line end. Col4 at 59px is the tightest column and carries the 4-digit total 1,115; col8 at 59px is also narrow.
critique.cause: Col1 at 123px gives 102px of text, crossing the threshold where 'Commercial &' fits on one line. Subtracting 3px from France Q1 and Australia Q1 creates the tight 59px numeric cells.

critique.good: The most balanced numeric rhythm of the three: Europe columns are 62px and Asia columns 60px. Col1 at 117px gives 96px of text, so 'Commercial' breaks before the ampersand. All 4-digit totals fit and all headers stay one line.
critique.problems: Europe spans 248px versus Asia-Pacific 240px, so the right half feels compressed. The 60px Asia columns are adequate but visibly tighter than Europe's 62px, especially with 4-digit totals 1,803 and 1,055.
critique.cause: The 8px difference comes from assigning 62px to cols 2–5 and 60px to cols 6–9 rather than equalizing the two four-column regions.

review.method: two fresh-context blind reviews; letters shuffled; includes browser auto layout and equal widths as neutral references

r1A.why: Clean hierarchy and readable row labels; words break only at spaces and all figures stay intact. The first column is slightly generous, leaving the numeric columns a little tighter than the best balance.

r2C.why: Figures and headers remain intact, but the row-header column is too narrow, forcing extra two-line wraps such as “Community solar” and “Residential rooftop”; the data columns are roomy.

ref_equal.why: The first column is collapsed: “Segment” splits as “Segm/ent” and row labels break mid-word (“Resid/ential”, “Com/merci/al”), making the table hard to scan.

ref_auto.why: No broken words and all numbers fit, but the row-header column dominates the table; the numeric columns are visibly compressed, weakening quarter-to-quarter comparison.

r1B.why: Best balance: the row header is just wide enough for the key labels, figures remain intact, and the numeric columns have even breathing room with a clear hierarchy.

r3A.why: Readable and intact, but the first column is wider than necessary, so the numeric columns are tighter than in E; still functional and clear.

raw.unsure: Exact column widths are hard to measure from the images; A/E/F differ only subtly, and I may misjudge borderline wraps such as “Community solar”.

ref_equal.why: Row-header column is starved: 'Segment' splits into 'Segm ent', and every row label fractures mid-word ('Resid ential rooftp', 'Com merci al & indust rial', 'Com munit y solar'), destroying the row units the table is scanned by.

r2C.why: Header column is wide enough for whole words; row labels wrap cleanly at spaces, numbers sit intact on one line, and the Europe/Asia-Pacific grouping reads clearly. Slightly wider first column than F but essentially sound.

r1A.why: Balanced widths, no broken words, all figures intact, group headers aligned over their quarters. Row labels wrap to two lines ('Community / solar') but remain readable; rhythm across the eight numeric columns is even.

r1B.why: Very similar to C: intact numbers, clean header hierarchy, sensible first-column width. Nothing broken, though the Segment column is a touch tight, forcing two-line labels on several rows.

r3A.why: Readable throughout with no split words and intact totals; the first column is marginally narrower than F so 'Community solar' wraps, giving slightly ragged row-header rhythm but no real scanning cost.

ref_auto.why: Best proportion: the Segment column holds 'Utility-scale' and 'Community solar' on single lines, row labels break only at natural spaces, all MW values align in evenly sized quarter columns, and the Germany/France/Japan/Australia pairs sit symmetrically under their region bands. Rows read as clean units.

raw.unsure: Layouts B–F differ only by a few pixels of first-column width, so my ranking among them rests on subtle wrapping differences visible in the row labels; I could not verify exact pixel sums against the 605px budget.

provenance.note: AI visual design judgement; not a human reading study
